title: Woman, 28, who died in London police custody was much more than just an addict: Brother
subtitle: Despite her own battle with substance abuse, Amanda Bolt worked to help others struggling with addictions and homelessness, said her older brother.
article: Despite her own battle with substance abuse, Amanda Bolt worked to help others struggling with addictions and homelessness, her older brother says.
Ontario's police watchdog identified Bolt, 28, as the woman who died in hospital Nov. 13 after being found unresponsive in a London police cell 10 days earlier.
Court records show Bolt, who had a history of run-ins with the law stretching back nearly a decade, was arrested on Nov. 2 and charged with failure to comply.
Sibling Chris Bolt acknowledged his younger sister was battling addiction "and the lifestyle that goes with it," but said that struggle didn't define her.
"Her entire life she was always one of the brightest in the room," he said.
Bolt participated in the London InterCommunity Health Centre's peer mentor program and was in the process of becoming a volunteer at London's needle exchange program, the elder Bolt said.
"She knew she could do good for other people," he said, adding his sister was a loved family member who should be remembered for the positive things she did in her life.

Bolt was found unresponsive in her cell the morning after her arrest. She was given naloxone - a nasal spray used to reverse the effects of opioid overdoses - before being taken to hospital where she died on Nov. 13, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said.

Neither police, paramedics nor the SIU would confirm who administered the naloxone, a drug London police officers have given to 111 people, 103 of whom survived, this year, according to statistics released earlier this month.
Police notified the SIU of the incident, but the watchdog initially said it was monitoring the woman's condition and hadn't invoked its mandate.

That changed on Monday when the SIU said the woman had died - Bolt's name wasn't released until Tuesday after her family gave the agency permission - though the SIU still hasn't specified how many officers are the subject of its probe.
Created in 1990, the SIU investigates all cases of serious injury, death and allegations of sexual assault involving police.
Bolt was scheduled to appear in a London courtroom on Tuesday on the failure to comply charge that led to her arrest, court records show.
Court records show a string of minor convictions dating back to 2012 for crimes including assault, mischief and theft.
In April, she was sentenced to 12 days' time served, 12 months' probation and given a 10-year weapons ban for an assault conviction, one of four assault convictions in the past seven years.
One of her longest stints in jail came in 2017, when she was sentenced to 47 days in pre-trial custody for theft. Other convictions resulted in short jail sentences, probation and fines.
Bolt's cause of death won't be made public until the SIU releases its final report to Ontario's attorney general, a process that takes at least several months.
Chris Bolt said his family is anxioius to find out the facts surrounding his sister's death, addding that her mistakes didn't define her.
"We're hoping that sooner rather than later some light will be shed on what actually happened," he said.
